title: ASAP: Attention Sink Anchored Pruning
claim: Prior token-reduction heuristics based on local scores keep background tokens and miss foreground; anchoring on the sink preserves salient objects.
layout: 2 rows by 6 columns, left-to-right, zoom lines into method comparison panel
description: Two example images are shown as rows: a girl blowing a bubble, and a coastal cliff. From left to right: the input photo, then an attention map overlay with a viridis colorbar. The map has a red dashed box marking the sink region and a green dotted box marking the foreground object. Black zoom lines connect this crop to a rounded gray panel. The panel holds four patch-grid visualizations, one per method: Local Cosine Similarity (ToMe), Local Attention (FastV/EViT), their combination (PPT), and Our Model (ASAP). Kept tokens appear as white-outlined colored tiles, merged or pruned regions are darkened, and a green overlay marks the foreground. Baselines scatter kept tokens over the background. ASAP's red-tinted grid keeps a coherent foreground and compresses the background. The eye goes first to the photos, then to the rightmost ASAP column.
caption: Visual comparison of token reduction under a fixed budget. Local cosine similarity (ToMe[ref]), local attention score (FastV[ref], EViT[ref]), and their combination (PPT[ref]) all fail to reliably separate foreground from background due to attention sink interference. Our method (ASAP) explicitly exploits the sink (red dashed) as a geometric anchor, consistently preserving key foreground objects (green dotted).
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) face severe computational bottlenecks due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention at high resolutions. Existing token reduction methods rely on local metrics -- such as single-layer attention scores -- that are inherently vulnerable to the attention sink phenomenon, where uninformative tokens are paradoxically preserved over salient foreground objects. We propose ASAP (Attention Sink Anchored Pruning), a training-free framework that recasts this sink as a feature. Modeling ViT information flow as a Lazy Random Walk, ASAP identifies the sink as a dominant accumulator of probability mass. By computing the diffusion distance to the sink within the cumulative transition matrix, ASAP partitions tokens via Radial Diffusion Clustering and compresses background redundancy through Transition Weight Pooling in a single shot. Extensive experiments across image, video, and vision-language tasks demonstrate ASAP outperforms state-of-the-art methods, accelerating throughput by up to 48% while maintaining or even exceeding baseline accuracy.
